content: Voriconazole and ergot derivatives (such as dihydroergotamine, ergonovine, ergotamine, and methylergonovine) are contraindicated with certain medications due to the risk of severe interactions. Cisapride and St. John's Wort are also known to interact adversely with these drugs. In the U.S. reference population from the Metropolitan Atlanta Congenital Defects Program (MACDP), the baseline rate of congenital defects is approximately 7%. However, the rate of miscarriage is not reported in the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR). The APR has methodological limitations, including the use of the MACDP as an external comparator group. The MACDP population is not disease-specific, evaluates women and infants from a limited geographic area, and does not include outcomes for births occurring before 20 weeks of gestation. Animal reproduction studies have shown that tipranavir can cause fetal toxicities at maternally toxic doses, with systemic exposures (AUC) lower than those observed in humans at the recommended human dose. Based on prospective reports to the APR and an Expanded Access program, approximately 17 live births were documented following exposure to tipranavir-containing regimens. Among these, 13 live births were exposed during the first trimester, and 4 during the second or third trimester. No birth defects were reported in the live-born infants. Tipranavir has been shown to cross the placenta. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommend that HIV-1-infected mothers in the United States avoid breastfeeding to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV-1. There is no information on the presence of tipranavir in human milk, its effects on breastfed infants, or its impact on milk production. However, tipranavir has been detected in rat milk. Due to the potential for HIV-1 transmission (in HIV-negative infants), the development of viral resistance (in HIV-positive patients), and possible adverse drug effects, mothers receiving tipranavir should not breastfeed. Tipranavir is classified as a protease inhibitor that prevents the cleavage of Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors, leading to the formation of immature, noninfectious viral particles. It must be co-administered with ritonavir to enhance its effectiveness. Tipranavir is not a cure for HIV infection but helps reduce the viral load, allowing the immune system to function more effectively. Patients must adhere strictly to their prescribed HIV medications to minimize the risk of spreading the virus to others. Barrier methods, such as latex or polyurethane condoms, should be used during sexual activity, and personal items that may come into contact with blood or body fluids should not be shared. Tipranavir capsules should be swallowed whole and taken at the same time as ritonavir, usually twice daily, as directed by a healthcare provider. It is crucial to maintain consistent dosing schedules and not to alter or discontinue the medication without medical advice. Common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, drowsiness, dizziness, headache, and vomiting. Patients should be aware that as their immune system strengthens, it may begin to fight off pre-existing infections, potentially causing symptoms to reappear. In rare cases, the immune system may become overactive, leading to inflammatory reactions. Changes in body fat distribution, such as increased fat in the upper back and abdomen and decreased fat in the arms and legs, may occur during treatment. The cause and long-term effects of these changes are unknown. Tipranavir can also cause mild rashes, which are usually not serious, but any rash should be evaluated by a healthcare provider to rule out severe allergic reactions. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies, including to sulfa drugs, and disclose all medications and supplements they are taking to avoid potential drug interactions. Tipranavir may cause dizziness or drowsiness, and alcohol or marijuana use can exacerbate these effects. Patients should avoid driving or operating machinery until they are sure they can do so safely. The medication may also increase blood sugar levels, potentially worsening or causing diabetes. Blood sugar should be monitored regularly, and any symptoms of hyperglycemia, such as increased thirst or urination, should be reported to a healthcare provider. Tipranavir may increase sensitivity to sunlight, so patients should limit sun exposure, use sunscreen, and wear protective clothing. During pregnancy, tipranavir should only be used when clearly needed, as it may reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to the baby. It is unknown whether tipranavir passes into breast milk. Drug interactions can alter the effectiveness of tipranavir or increase the risk of side effects. Patients should maintain a list of all medications and supplements they use and share it with their healthcare provider. Certain drugs, such as apalutamide, macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), and rifampin, can affect the removal of tipranavir from the body. Tipranavir, when combined with ritonavir, can also alter the metabolism of other drugs. Aspirin may increase the risk of bleeding when used with tipranavir, but low-dose aspirin prescribed for cardiovascular prevention should not be discontinued without medical advice. Hormonal birth control methods may be less effective when used with tipranavir, so alternative or backup contraception methods should be discussed with a healthcare provider. In case of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. U.S. residents can contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222. Regular medical and laboratory tests, including liver function, HIV RNA levels, blood sugar, and cholesterol, should be conducted during treatment. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next scheduled dose. Unopened bottles of tipranavir capsules should be stored in the refrigerator, and once opened, they can be kept at room temperature for up to 60 days. Proper disposal of expired or unused medication is essential.
